reader.title: Lynching of "Arizona Bill" at Pittman Valley
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An armed party took a prisoner held for killing a man from a deputy sheriff's custody and hanged and shot him (A1, A2, A4).

A party of about forty (A2) or about 200 (A1) armed men took Bill from a deputy's guard and hanged and shot him for killing Collins, with no lawful authority (A1, A2, A4); no paper gives his race, so the anti-Black scope is unsupported (see flags).

Two Prescott papers (A1, A2), a resident's letter (A4) and the New York Police News via Wheeling (A5) independently agree that Bill shot Collins and was taken from custody, hanged and shot, though details differ.

summary.text: The lynching of "Arizona Bill" took place at Pittman Valley, Arizona Territory, around Christmas Day 1881, when an armed party took the man, named by Prescott papers as William Lewis, from a deputy sheriff's guard and hanged and shot him.
He was accused of shooting Charles Collins, known as "Shorty", during a quarrel, and the story travelled from Prescott papers to Tombstone, Los Angeles, Iowa and West Virginia.

Pittman Valley, called "Pittman's Flat" by the Prescott Miner, was a small settlement on the Atlantic and Pacific railroad line, twenty-three miles from Flagstaff, where railroad construction crews were at work.
Bill was a local lawman, described variously as a deputy sheriff, a county deputy marshal and a deputy U.S. marshal.
On Christmas Day, as two men quarrelled in front of Nellis' saloon, Collins came up with his pistol in hand and demanded fair play, and Bill shot him dead.
According to the Arizona Democrat, a crowd gathered and talked of lynching, and when Bill barricaded himself in a log cabin they dug beneath it, laid Judson powder and set a fuse.
Deputy Sheriff Ed Whipple arrived in time to stop the explosion and persuaded Bill to surrender on a promise that he would be taken to Prescott for trial.
Bill was held under guard in a building, Price & King's office in the Democrat's account, and a resident's letter says an inquest the next day sustained the accusation against him.
An armed party then came for him, about forty men by the Democrat's count and about 200 railroad men by the Miner's, and the guard gave him up.
They took him to a tree close by, hanged him from a limb and fired into his body as he strangled, fourteen shots according to the Miner.
Whipple buried Bill, and the Democrat said he had trouble getting a grave dug and a coffin made because feeling against Bill ran so high.
No report of an inquest into Bill's death, or of any arrest of the lynchers, appears in the coverage.

The Arizona papers reported the lynching as local news without comment on its lawlessness; the Miner's version, reprinted in Los Angeles, admitted that the particulars were "very meagre and unsatisfactory."
The Democrat's account, reprinted in the Tombstone Epitaph, ended by recalling Bill as "an efficient officer."

J. P. Davies, writing to an Iowa paper, explained the killing by the railroaders' temper, saying "vengeance is speedy and terrible" when their hatred was roused, called Bill "the victim of lynch law" and blamed drink.
A Wheeling column, citing the New York Police News, focused on Collins as a possible local son and called Bill "a desperate character."
None of the papers mentioned the race of either man.
The Prescott papers named the lynched man William Lewis, while the Wheeling report called him William Monroe.
The Democrat placed the lynching on Christmas evening after the crowd had gone to supper, but the Miner, the letter and the Wheeling report put it on the following day.

accounts.label: Arizona Democrat (Prescott)
accounts.gist: Bill shot Collins, held off a crowd in a cabin until Whipple took his surrender on a promise of trial at Prescott; that evening forty armed men took him from Price & King's office and hanged and shot him.

accounts.label: Prescott Miner
accounts.gist: Lewis shot Collins without apparent reason, was held overnight under guard, and on Monday morning about 200 armed railroad men took him from the guard, hanged him to a tree and fired fourteen shots into him.

accounts.label: Resident's letter
accounts.gist: After an inquest, Bill was in a deputy sheriff's charge when Shorty's comrades surrounded the building; the guard yielded and he was hanged and shot by moonlight.

accounts.label: New York Police News via Wheeling
accounts.gist: Shorty's friends took 'Arizona Bill', a deputy U.S. marshal, from the jail the following day, hanged him and riddled his body.

framing.detail: The Prescott Miner reprint ran it among 'Arizona News' and called the particulars 'very meagre and unsatisfactory'.
The Arizona Democrat, reprinted in the Epitaph, told the mob's siege and the lynching plainly, stressed the feeling against Bill, and closed by calling him an efficient officer.
The Iowa letter explained the lynching by the railroaders' vengeance, called Bill 'the victim of lynch law' and blamed drink.
The Wheeling column treated it as news of a local son's death, calling Bill 'a desperate character'.

conflicts.note: Both Prescott papers give Lewis; Monroe comes only from a secondhand eastern report.
